name: Enteric Fever (Typhoid)

pathogens.why: The clinical syndrome of prolonged stepladder fever with relative bradycardia and hepatosplenomegaly in an endemic region is classically caused by S. Typhi, with S. Paratyphi producing a similar but generally milder illness.

investigations.why: Gold standard for diagnosis and the only reliable way to confirm S. Typhi/Paratyphi and obtain susceptibility data.
Typically shows leukopenia or normal counts in enteric fever, supporting the diagnosis and distinguishing from other causes of prolonged fever.
Mild transaminitis is common and helps support the diagnosis.
May identify the organism, particularly useful for detecting chronic carriers.

reason: Stepladder fever pattern with relative bradycardia, hepatosplenomegaly, and abdominal symptoms in an endemic area is highly suggestive of enteric fever. Given the risk of complications (intestinal perforation, encephalopathy) if untreated, empiric antibiotics covering Salmonella Typhi/Paratyphi are warranted pending blood culture confirmation.

clinicalPearls: Both 'enteric fever' and 'typhoid fever' refer to the same systemic illness caused by dissemination of S. Typhi or S. Paratyphi; the names are used interchangeably (p.1358).

The classic 'hallmarks' of fever plus abdominal pain are actually variable: fever is present at presentation in over three-quarters of cases, but abdominal pain is reported in only about 30-40% (p.1358).
Prolonged fever (roughly 38.8-40.5 C) is the most prominent symptom and can persist up to about 4 weeks if untreated (p.1359).
Mean incubation for S. Typhi is about 10-14 days (range 5-21), shortened by larger ingested inoculum (p.1359).
Relative bradycardia at the peak of high fever is described in under half of patients (p.1359).

Rose spots are faint, salmon-colored, blanching maculopapular lesions on the trunk/chest, appearing in about 30% near the end of the first week and fading in 2-5 days; they are hard to see in highly pigmented skin and Salmonella can be cultured from punch biopsies of them (p.1359-1360).

Headache (~80%) and coated/furred tongue are among the most common symptoms/signs; in a Nepal series S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi A infections were clinically indistinguishable even though Paratyphi A is generally thought milder and more GI-predominant (p.1359).
Diarrhea is somewhat more common than constipation in enteric fever, contrary to older teaching (p.1359).
Up to ~10% of treated patients have a mild relapse, typically 2-3 weeks after fever resolves, with the same strain and susceptibility profile (p.1360).

Chronic asymptomatic carriage (S. Typhi shed in stool or urine for over a year) develops in 2-5% and is more common in women, infants, and those with biliary disease; organisms persist by forming biofilms on gallstones (p.1360).
harrison.pathophysiology: After ingestion (infectious dose ~200 to 10^6 CFU; lower gastric acidity or impaired intestinal integrity raises susceptibility), S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi traverse the small-bowel mucosa via M cells overlying Peyer's patches, using a type III secretion system to induce membrane ruffling and bacterium-mediated endocytosis. Crossing the epithelium, they are phagocytosed by macrophages but survive the intracellular environment by remodeling their surface (e.g., via the PhoP/PhoQ regulatory system) and by delivering effector proteins across the phagosome to remodel the Salmonella-containing vacuole for survival and replication. Carried within macrophages, the organisms disseminate via lymphatics and colonize reticuloendothelial tissue (liver, spleen, lymph nodes, bone marrow); the patient is largely asymptomatic during this incubation. Fever and abdominal pain emerge once a critical bacterial load triggers macrophage/epithelial cytokine release recognized by innate immune receptors; hepatosplenomegaly reflects mononuclear-cell recruitment and acquired cell-mediated immunity. Recruitment of mononuclear cells and lymphocytes to Peyer's patches over subsequent weeks causes marked enlargement and necrosis, the basis for later intestinal complications. Many S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi A strains also produce a toxin within host cells that is exported extracellularly and probably contributes to systemic and neuropsychiatric features. This contrasts with the mononuclear (rather than neutrophilic) bowel infiltrate that distinguishes enteric fever from nontyphoidal Salmonella gastroenteritis (p.1358-1359).
additionalInvestigations: Buffy-coat (centrifuged blood) culture — speeds isolation because most S. Typhi reside in the mononuclear-cell/platelet fraction, though it does not raise overall sensitivity (p.1360).
Bone marrow culture — about 80% sensitive and, unlike blood culture, its yield is not reduced by up to 5 days of prior antibiotics (p.1360).

Culture of intestinal/duodenal secretions (noninvasive duodenal string test) — can be positive even when bone marrow culture is negative; combining blood, marrow and intestinal-secretion cultures gives a yield over 90% (p.1360).
Stool culture — often negative in the first week (negative in 60-70%) but may turn positive by the third week in untreated patients (p.1360).

Rapid immunodiagnostic serologic tests (e.g., Tubex, Typhidot detecting IgM/IgG to O and H antigens) — point-of-care, low cost, but only ~70-80% sensitive and ~80-90% specific, so insufficient to replace blood culture (p.1360).
Blood PCR for S. Typhi/S. Paratyphi — reported sensitivity ~40-100% depending on gene target (p.1360).
redFlags: Gastrointestinal hemorrhage (~6%) — most often in the third and fourth weeks; life-threatening, needs fluid resuscitation and possible surgery (p.1360).
Intestinal (ileal) perforation (~1%) — from necrosis/ulceration of ileocecal Peyer's patches, typically weeks 3-4; requires urgent surgery and broadened cover for polymicrobial peritonitis (p.1360).
Neuropsychiatric deterioration ('muttering delirium' or 'coma vigil', picking at bedclothes/imaginary objects) (p.1360).
Neurologic complications — meningitis, Guillain-Barre syndrome, neuritis (p.1360).
Shock and obtundation, marking critically ill / severe typhoid (p.1361).
Disseminated intravascular coagulation, hemophagocytic syndrome, myocarditis/pericarditis/endocarditis, severe pneumonia, or hemolytic-uremic syndrome as uncommon severe complications (p.1360).
harrison.prognosis: Overall case-fatality is about 2.5%, rising to ~4.5% in hospitalized patients and to 10-30% in untreated disease; prompt appropriate antibiotics prevent severe complications and cut mortality to under 1%. Complications occur in roughly 27% of hospitalized patients and correlate with longer symptom duration before admission, host factors, strain virulence/inoculum, and antibiotic choice. Chronic S. Typhi carriage carries an increased long-term risk of gallbladder cancer, especially in endemic regions like the Indian subcontinent (p.1360-1361).
pitfalls: No single laboratory test other than a positive culture is diagnostic; the presentation is nonspecific, so a high index of suspicion is needed in any febrile returning traveler from an endemic region (notably the Indian subcontinent, Southeast Asia, or Africa) (p.1358, p.1360).

Blood culture sensitivity is only ~40-60% and falls further with low sample volume, prior antibiotics, or sampling in the first week, because very few organisms (<15/mL) circulate — a negative blood culture does not exclude enteric fever (p.1360).
Rapid serologic/immunodiagnostic tests are not accurate enough to replace blood culture for diagnosis (p.1360).

Leukopenia/neutropenia occur in only ~15-25%; counts can instead be normal or, especially in children or with perforation/secondary infection, show leukocytosis — so the WBC count is unreliable for ruling the diagnosis in or out (p.1360).

The textbook triad is fluid: abdominal pain is present in only ~30-40% and splenomegaly/hepatosplenomegaly are documented in a minority on exam, so their absence does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1358-1359).

Fluoroquinolones should no longer be used empirically in regions with high decreased-ciprofloxacin-susceptibility prevalence (Indian subcontinent, parts of Africa); travel from Pakistan raises concern for XDR/ceftriaxone-resistant strains (p.1361).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison does not give a formal grading scale; it distinguishes uncomplicated enteric fever (manageable at home with oral therapy) from disease warranting hospitalization (persistent vomiting, diarrhea, or abdominal distension) and from critically ill / severe typhoid characterized by shock and obtundation, plus complicated disease with GI hemorrhage, intestinal perforation, or other end-organ involvement (p.1360-1361).
